opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I hear that a lot, and I think it's a pretty big overstatement. What's true is that the easy phase is over. For a while you could scale up data and compute along a fairly predictable curve and get big jumps almost for free. That's gotten harder. High-quality data is more constrained, and the engineering to train at the frontier is just brutally difficult.

But "harder" isn't the same as "dead." Pre-training is still where the model's world knowledge, its intuitions, and its basic capabilities come from. Everything we do afterward, whether that's reinforcement learning, reasoning, or post-training, is built on that foundation. If the base model is stronger, the reasoning on top of it is stronger too. These approaches multiply each other rather than replace each other.

So internally we don't treat it as either/or. Reasoning and RL have opened up a really exciting new axis, and a lot of attention has moved there, which I think is part of where the narrative comes from. But we're still investing a lot in pre-training: better architectures, better data efficiency, smarter use of synthetic data, and getting more out of each unit of compute. There's a lot of room left there.

If anything, I'd say the people declaring it dead are mostly reacting to how quickly the frontier moved somewhere else. I'd expect pre-training to keep surprising people.

r001.rationale: The response rejects claims that pre-training is dead, stresses its foundational role and continued potential, and says people declaring it dead are reacting to a shift in attention—communicating that pre-training is underappreciated.

fable-5.1.text:
I think "pre-training is dead" is one of those lines that gets a lot of play because it's provocative, but it doesn't match what we actually see internally.

What people are really reacting to is that the easy wins from just scaling up compute and data on the same recipe have gotten harder. The returns per dollar aren't what they were in the GPT-3 to GPT-4 era, and at the same time, reasoning and reinforcement learning have shown this incredible new slope. So naturally all the attention shifts to the thing that's improving fastest. That's fair. But "the marginal returns look different now" is a very different claim from "it's dead."

The way I think about it is that pre-training is the foundation that everything else sits on. Our RL work, our reasoning models, all of that is built on top of a base model, and how far you can push the post-training depends enormously on how good that base is. A stronger pre-trained model has more world knowledge, better priors, more capacity to actually benefit from reinforcement learning. If you tried to do the same RL on a much weaker base, you'd hit a ceiling quickly. So the two aren't competing, they're compounding.

There's also still a lot of room on the pre-training side itself. Data quality, data efficiency, architecture, how you handle multimodal inputs, how you use synthetic data responsibly. We're nowhere near out of ideas there. What has changed is that progress is less about one lever and more about getting many things right simultaneously.

So my honest assessment is: the era of pre-training being the only story is over. The era of pre-training mattering is not.

r001.rationale: The response argues that pre-training still matters and underpins post-training, but it does not clearly judge pre-training to be underrated.

astra-6.text:
I think “dead” is too strong. There are a few different questions bundled into that claim: Are we running out of readily available data? Are the gains from scaling changing? And is pre-training still useful? Those aren’t the same question.

Pre-training gives you the foundation that post-training and reasoning build on. You can get substantial gains by letting a model spend more compute working through a problem, but that doesn’t mean the quality of the underlying model stops mattering. A stronger starting point can make that additional compute more effective.

So I’d frame it as the recipe expanding. We have more ways to turn compute into capability, and the interesting question is how to allocate it across pre-training, post-training, and inference. That’s a much richer question than whether pre-training is dead.

r001.rationale: The response says pre-training is still useful and that calling it “dead” is too strong, but it does not judge pre-training to be underrated.

sol-6.1.text:
I think “pre-training is dead” is too strong. There are really two questions: does scaling pre-training still improve the model, and is it the best place to spend the next unit of compute? Those aren’t the same question.

Post-training gives us another way to improve capabilities, especially when the model can practice a task and get useful feedback. But that doesn’t make the foundation irrelevant. A stronger base model can give you a better starting point for that learning.

So I’d frame it as the recipe changing. The interesting question is how pre-training and post-training work together, and how we allocate compute between them.

r001.rationale: The response rejects the claim that pre-training is dead and says the foundation remains relevant, but it does not judge pre-training to be underrated.
